title: Should a plant be able to inherit a body plan that doesn't work?
question: Two questions, and the second is the one I need. (1) Do these two swards look meaningfully different to you, and is either better? (2) A plant's growth program is now inherited and mutates, but there is a safety net: when a mutation removes a rule, the plant silently falls back on its species' original rule and grows exactly as before. Taking that net away is what B is. It makes mutation able to reach new forms — and able to hand a lineage a plant that cannot grow. Do you want the net or not?
context_md:
**The mutation rate is turned up 50x in both panes.** At the shipped rate these two are indistinguishable — that is measured, not assumed, and it is half the answer: the fork changes nothing until the rate rises too. They are one seed and one pair, and spread here is enormous, so treat the picture as evidence and not as a result.

**A — the net (what ships).** A mutation that removes a rule is absorbed and the plant grows as before.

**B — no net.** The genome answers, full stop.

**What is measured, separately, by census:**

| | |
|---|---|
| removing a rule changes the plant today (tree) | **0%** — 0 of 40, at three world seeds |
| the *middle* option (drop the species table, keep the engine default) | **inert** — byte-identical to A at 10x rate |
| plants killed outright by B in these runs | **none seen** |

The thing I expected to see in B was a graveyard. It is not one. That is why this is worth your eye rather than my judgement.

items.label: A — the safety net (ships today)
items.caption: a removed rule falls back on the species' original
